Issued at 149 AM MDT Wed Oct 7 2026

Classic rock was on the docket for tonight's shift and I heard 
two songs that describe my feelings about the upcoming weather 
over the next several days and what will happen. With the nice 
autumn weather we have had over the past several days that I 
have been really enjoying, my feelings were related to the song
"Don't Change" by INXS, especially the line "Don't Change a 
Thing". However, reality will be related to the other song I 
heard, "Changes" by the late, great David Bowie, as we will have
a major change in the pattern coming this weekend and early 
next week. 

It will be more of the same through Friday though. Ridging will 
continue to hold fairly strong through this time, with 700 millibar 
temperatures remaining at 10 Celsius or higher through this 
period, resulting in a continuation of well above normal 
temperatures. Most locations at 5500 feet or lower have at least
a 1 in 2 chance of high temperatures over 80 degrees each 
afternoon through this period. There is another concern for 
Friday though, fire weather. An approaching cold front, the one 
that will likely change the pattern, will be toward Montana. 
This will tighten the pressure gradient across the area, with 
the strongest wind gust in the favored southwest flow areas, 
like from Rock Springs through Casper. A large portion of the 
area has at least a 1 in 2 chance of wind gusts past 30 mph, 
with the windier areas having at least a 3 out of 4 chance of 
gusts past 40 mph. The limiting factor will be humidity though. 
As of now, the portions of the Bighorn Basin as well as Johnson 
and Natrona Counties have a mean low relative humidity of 15 
percent or lower. If we need fire weather highlights, this is 
where they would likely be. However, at least elevated fire 
weather will be possible across most of the area. This also 
looks like the warmest day with the downsloping flow, with some 
areas possibly seeing highs over 85 degrees. As for 
precipitation, we can't completely rule out a stray shower or 
storm over southern Sweetwater County. However, with the chance 
generally 1 out of 10 or less, the forecast was left dry for the
most part.

Saturday looks like the transition day as we enter a wetter and a 
rather complicated pattern as we head through the weekend and even 
into next week. We have three main players with this. The first is 
the cold front, the strongest so far this season by far, that will 
be dropping toward Wyoming. The second is an upper level low moving 
in from the northwest. And the third will be some tropical moisture 
moving toward the area from Tropical Cyclone Rachel. How these 
interact and when they interact will ultimately determine where
the heaviest precipitation will fall, when it will fall and 
what type of precipitation will fall. There are some details on 
each one in the following paragraphs.

Uncertainty #1: How fast and how far will the colder air move into 
Wyoming. It should remain north of Wyoming for most of Saturday, 
bringing another warm day although a bit cooler than on Friday. 
Sunday is where there is a decent amount of model divergence with 
how cold it will get. For example, the ECMWF model is more 
aggressive and pushes the front down to the Continental Divide, 
with 700 millibar temperatures much lower on Sunday. The 0 
Celsius line makes it down to the Divide, which would lower 
snow levels down to around 8500 feet. Northern portions of the 
state would get as low as minus 6C, which could bring some snow
into areas like Cody Sunday into Sunday night. Meanwhile, the 
GFS is much warmer, keeping snow levels anywhere from 1000 to 
2000 feet higher, which would be mainly in the mountains. So, 
there is still a ton of uncertainty in regards to this.

Uncertainty #2: The exact track of the moisture plume from the 
remnants of Rachel as it interacts with the upper level low and the 
cold front. Recent trends have pulled things a bit further west, 
with the highest amounts in the western mountains, especially in 
areas prone to southwest flow, like the Wind River Range. There is 
decent agreement in the Sunday afternoon and Sunday night time
period when the heaviest precipitation moves across the area. 
But, with it being several days out, this is subject to change. 
Precipitable water values do rise to over 150 percent of normal 
at times, so some heavier precipitation is possible at times.

Uncertainty #3: How fast the system move out of the area. Guidance 
is all over the place with a trailing upper level low that could 
bring some additional showers next week. The guidance is all over 
the place in regards to this but unsettled weather could linger into 
the middle of next week as well.
